route.title: Commission and Counter-Movement
route.marker: The word-event formula and rise-go commission open the book; Jonah's matching rise-to-flee and repeated descent complete the commission-response movement before Yahweh initiates the storm in 1:4.
route.rationale: Jonah 1:1-3 is a complete initiating scene because the narrated counter-movement is the response to the commission, while 1:4 changes agent, setting pressure, and action to the sea crisis.
route.rejected: Splitting 1:1-2 from 1:3 would detach the command from its narrated answer; extending through 1:6 would cross from flight into the independently staged storm-and-captain encounter.
route.basis: Commission formula, imperative speech, mirrored rise verb, directional flight, and the new divine storm action yield a strong close and reset.
route.counter: The direct commission closes syntactically at 1:2, so a speech-only child is possible, but it would weaken the commission-response form.
route.guard: No motive, identity, authorship, date, history, or genre-historicity ruling follows from the commission-flight structure.

route.title: Storm Escalation and Captain's Summons
route.marker: Yahweh's storm action opens a new crisis; sailor fear, cargo action, Jonah's enclosed sleep, and the captain's rise-call appeal bring the storm into direct encounter with Jonah before collective lot-taking begins at 1:7.
route.rationale: The external storm tableau and Jonah's sleep are joined by the captain's complete wake-up speech; 1:7 then changes to a collective diagnostic procedure.
route.rejected: Separating 1:4-5 from 1:6 would isolate the captain's response from the storm and sleep that occasion it; merging through 1:10 would erase the lot-and-identity inquiry movement.
route.basis: New divine action, escalating ship crisis, spatial contrast, captain arrival, echoed rise-call language, and the procedural reset at 1:7 support the unit.
route.counter: Verse 6 is a compact direct speech with difficult idiom and could be surfaced alone if the scene were always hydrated.
route.guard: Do not infer sailor spiritual status, ethnic comparison, miracle mechanism, or a fixed rendering of the ship and captain idioms from this boundary.

route.title: Lot Inquiry and Identity Disclosure
route.marker: The collective lot proposal and result open a forensic sequence; clustered questions receive Jonah's self-identification, and the sailors' great fear and causal reaction close the discovery before the remedy question at 1:11.
route.rationale: Lot, interrogation, answer, disclosed flight, and fearful consequence form one cause-identification movement that is complete when 1:11 shifts from who caused the crisis to what action should be taken.
route.rejected: Splitting 1:7, 1:8, and 1:9-10 would separate procedure, questions, answer, and reaction; merging with 1:11-16 would conflate discovery with crisis resolution.
route.basis: Collective proposal, lot result, question cluster, first-person identity answer, causal disclosure, and the new remedy interrogative provide strong dialogue boundaries.
route.counter: Verses 7 and 8 begin distinct speech acts, and 1:10 is narrated reaction rather than part of Jonah's answer.
route.guard: Identity language and lot procedure do not authorize biography, spiritual ranking, ethnic comparison, or an account of divine causation.

route.title: Remedy, Resisted Casting, Calm, and Sailor Response
route.marker: The remedy question opens the sequence; Jonah's prescription, failed rowing alternative, prayer, casting, calm, fear, sacrifice, and vows enact and resolve the proposed remedy through 1:16.
route.rationale: The scene preserves both the sailors' resistance and the full action-result-aftermath chain, reaching closure only after the calm produces their reported response.
route.rejected: Ending at 1:12 would detach proposal from enactment; splitting prayer at 1:14 or calm at 1:15 from 1:16 would sever the crisis resolution from its immediate aftermath.
route.basis: Remedy consultation, prescribed action, counterattempt, collective prayer, execution, environmental resolution, and communal aftermath form a complete narrative arc.
route.counter: The prayer and the casting-calm climax are real internal submovements, and 1:16 could be treated as an aftermath child under hydration.
route.guard: Sacrifice and vows do not establish conversion or salvific status; the boundary decides no miracle mechanics or violence ethic.

route.title: Appointed-Fish Enclosure and Prayer Frame
route.marker: The appointed fish, temporal enclosure, and prayer from inside the fish form one prose frame across the WEB chapter seam; in WLC coordinates these are Jonah 2:1-2.
route.rationale: The appointment establishes the location and duration from which Jonah's prayer is introduced, so the English chapter boundary remains internal while 2:2 begins the quoted psalmic prayer.
route.rejected: A standalone 1:17 would turn the fish notice into a proof text; attaching 2:1 to the poem would separate its narratorial speech introduction from the narrative frame that locates it.
route.basis: Repeated narrative action, cross-versification alignment, prayer-introduction syntax, and the prose-to-poetry shift at 2:2 support the two-verse frame.
route.counter: WEB prints a chapter boundary after 1:17, and 2:1 begins a new explicit action; fish gender wording and three-days language remain translation pressures.
route.guard: The WEB-to-WLC crosswalk and fish wording are evidence only and decide no miracle mechanism, chronology, identity, or genre-historicity question.

route.title: Prayer from Distress to Thanksgiving
route.marker: Introduced first-person speech moves through distress and answer, engulfment and descent imagery, remembered address, vow and thanksgiving, and the closing acclamation; WLC-family samekh after 2:9 corroborates the close.
route.rationale: The embedded poem has a complete internal arc whose parallelism and imagistic movement should remain together, while 2:10 returns to third-person narration and fish action.
route.rejected: Dividing at 2:4, 2:7, or 2:8 would elevate internal poetic turns into autonomous chunks; merging 2:10 would cross the explicit poem-to-narrative form reset.
route.basis: Speech framing, first-person poetic parallelism, coherent descent-to-recollection-to-vow movement, final acclamation, and a narratorial reset make the poem a strong literary unit.
route.counter: Verses 2:4, 2:7, and 2:8 are genuine internal turns, and Psalm-like parallels can tempt smaller retrieval units.
route.guard: Psalm parallels establish form only, not quotation, compilation, source, dependence direction, doctrine, or a prayer-result rule.

route.title: Narrative Deliverance Exit Frame
route.marker: Third-person narration resumes as Yahweh addresses the fish and the fish deposits Jonah on dry land; WLC-family pe after the corresponding verse corroborates closure before the renewed word-event in 3:1.
route.rationale: The one-verse exit frame is a real speaker-and-form reset that closes the fish-prayer complex, but it is retrievable only with mandatory 1:17-2:10 parent hydration.
route.rejected: Merging it into the prayer would erase the narrator resumption; merging it into 3:1-4 would make deliverance merely recommission preparation and detach it from the fish-prayer frame.
route.basis: Narrator resumption, new agent action, dry-land endpoint, textual paragraph close, and the later word-event reset support the closure despite its brevity.
route.counter: The verse has no independent discourse development and could be retained only as the closing sentence of the larger fish-prayer parent.
route.guard: Mandatory Jonah 1:17-2:10 hydration; no standalone miracle-mechanism, automatic answered-prayer, history, or theology claim.

route.title: Recommission, Obedience, and Proclamation
route.marker: The repeated word-event and rise-go commission are answered by Jonah's matching rise and obedience, and the movement culminates in the proclaimed message before citywide response begins at 3:5.
route.rationale: Commission, obedient travel, city entry, and proclamation belong together because the quoted message is the enacted endpoint of the command; 3:5 changes agent and action to reception.
route.rejected: Splitting 3:1-3 from 3:4 would detach commission and travel from the proclamation they enable; extending through 3:10 would merge messenger action with the city's response and outcome.
route.basis: Repeated formula, mirrored rise-go verbs, explicit obedience, arrival frame, quoted proclamation, and response reset yield a strong scene child.
route.counter: The compact proclamation in 3:4 is a complete quoted speech and could be isolated if the whole scene were obligatorily hydrated.
route.guard: City measure, chronology, historicity, message fulfillment, and relation to later canonical reuse remain undecided.

route.title: City Response, Royal Decree, Turning, and Outcome
route.marker: Citywide belief and fasting expand through the king's enacted response and formally introduced decree; the contingency question is answered by the narrator's observed turning and reported outcome in 3:10.
route.rationale: Population response, royal response, decree, enacted turning, and narrative result form a deliberate cause-response close, so the speech-to-narration change at 3:9-10 remains internal.
route.rejected: Splitting 3:5-6, 3:7-9, and 3:10 would isolate the decree from its enactment and turn the result verse into a divine-relenting proof text.
route.basis: Escalating social scope, quoted decree, imperative turning chain, contingency question, repeated turn language, and narrator outcome bind the scene.
route.counter: The decree is a bounded quoted legal form, and 3:10 is a strong third-person narrative conclusion that could surface under mandatory parent hydration.
route.guard: Do not infer Ninevite covenantal or salvific status, conditional-prophecy doctrine, divine psychology, ethics, chronology, or source direction.

route.title: Anger-Prayer and Divine Counterquestion
route.marker: Narrated displeasure and anger trigger a complaint-prayer and death request, answered by the divine counterquestion at 4:4; the booth scene opens with a spatial action reset at 4:5.
route.rationale: Jonah's anger is interpreted by his own complaint and receives an immediate dialogue response, making 4:4 the close of the exchange rather than a detachable aphorism.
route.rejected: Splitting 4:1-3 from 4:4 would separate complaint from answer; attaching 4:5 would cross from dialogue into a new enacted setting and watch posture.
route.basis: Emotion report, explicit prayer, retrospective explanation, death request, responding question, and new spatial scene strongly frame the exchange.
route.counter: WLC-family samekh after 4:3 marks a real internal pressure, and 4:4 is a compact complete speech.
route.guard: The repeated evil/calamity and anger vocabulary decides no divine psychology, immutability question, ethics, motive, or doctrinal proposition.

route.title: Booth and Appointed-Agent Object Lesson
route.marker: Jonah's departure, booth, and watch posture establish the enacted setting; repeated appointment of plant, worm, and wind produces reversal and bodily collapse through the renewed death wish at 4:8.
route.rationale: The booth frame and three appointed agents form one staged object lesson whose final distress supplies the condition interpreted by the renewed dialogue at 4:9.
route.rejected: Separating each appointed agent would atomize a cumulative reversal sequence; including 4:9 would cross from enacted object lesson to explicit interpretive dialogue.
route.basis: New setting, repeated appointment formula, growth-withering-wind sequence, physical consequence, and dialogue reset create a coherent narrative unit.
route.counter: The plant, worm, and wind are individually marked appointments, and Jonah's direct speech in 4:8 could be read as the opening turn of the final dialogue.
route.guard: Plant identity, east-wind wording including the rendering range of the Hebrew term at 4:8, miracle mechanism, and ethics remain translation or retrieval questions only.

route.title: Renewed Anger Dialogue and Open Pity Question
route.marker: The repeated anger question opens the exchange; Jonah's answer is met by the vine-to-city pity comparison, which closes the book as an unanswered interrogative.
route.rationale: Question, reply, countercomparison, and final open question are inseparable dialogue turns; preserving the unanswered close prevents an imposed ethical or theological answer.
route.rejected: Separating 4:9 from 4:10-11 would detach prompt and reply from their interpretation; isolating 4:11 would strip the final question of the vine comparison.
route.basis: Repeated dialogue formula, direct reply, second-person/first-person comparison, and deliberately unanswered interrogative produce a strong closing unit.
route.counter: Jonah's answer in 4:9 is a complete speech, while 4:10 begins a new divine speech and 4:11 could be treated as its climactic sentence.
route.guard: Do not supply Jonah's answer or decide divine psychology, city ethics, fulfillment, animal theology, final-number interpretation, or canonical application.

dissents.rationale: The WEB chapter seam remains visible but is rejected as a surface boundary because the fish appointment and prayer introduction form one cross-versification prose frame.
The one-verse deliverance frame remains dependent on mandatory 1:17-2:10 hydration but is preserved because speaker, form, action, and WLC paragraph evidence reset after the prayer.
The decree and narrative outcome are real internal forms, but the contingency question and observed turning bind them into the complete city-response movement.
The WLC-family paragraph mark after 4:3 is preserved as counterevidence, but 4:4 completes the dialogue response before the booth scene.
